items.headline: Rendezvous Robotics raises $20M to build self‑assembling spacecraft
items.title: Exclusive: Rendezvous Robotics Raises $20M to Develop Self-Assembling Spacecraft
items.scifi_hook: A Colorado startup will launch modular tiles that snap together in orbit like space origami.
items.eli5: Tiny hexagonal spacecraft pieces will use magnets to join themselves into a full satellite after launch.
items.why: It could shrink launch costs by fitting larger satellites into existing rockets.
items.text: Rendezvous Robotics, the CO-based startup developing self-assembling spacecraft, announced $20M in fresh funding today to support an in-space demo launching NET April 2028. MaC Venture Capital and Toyota Ventures led the round, which included additional participation from the University of Michigan Endowment, Astera Ventures, Industrious Ventures, Aurelia Foundry, ATX Venture Partners, Mana Ventures and others. Too big to fly: Satellites are rapidly outgrowing the rockets that can take them to orbit. Across the industry, satellite manufacturers are developing sats that require football-field-sized solar arrays and large-aperture antennas—neither of which fit comfortably inside available rocket fairings. For many, the solution to this size mismatch looks like origami. But Rendezvous Robotics is taking a different approach—developing technology to allow future satellites to launch in pieces that can self-assemble in space. The technology builds off nearly a decade of research by cofounder Ariel Ekblaw under the TESSERAE program, which began at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Rendezvous Robotics’ version is a series of ~1 m hexagonal tiles—each equipped with sensors and onboard processing capabilities. Together, these tiles use electromagnetic fields to self-assemble in the vacuum of space. items.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5043-5049: Preparing to Drill at ‘Nazca’

MAHLI, located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm, uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different focus positions, to bring multiple features into focus in a single image. Curiosity composed the image on Oct. 18, 2026, Sol 5048 (Martian day 5,048 of the Mars Science Laboratory Mission), at 12:19:51 UTC. items.headline: Qarakal Quantum and Quantum Elements win $2.4M BIRD grant for chemistry simulation platform
items.title: Qarakal Quantum And Quantum Elements Receive BIRD Foundation Grant For Quantum Computing Innovation With a $2.4 Million Budget
items.scifi_hook: Superconducting qubits team up with digital twins to model reactions on material surfaces.
items.eli5: They will use special quantum computers and software to mimic how chemicals react on surfaces.
items.why: Advances could speed catalyst design and reduce costly lab experiments.
items.text: Insider Brief Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum were selected by the BIRD Foundation for a $2.4 million project to develop a quantum simulation platform for chemical reactions on material surfaces. The collaboration will combine Qarakal’s superconducting quantum hardware with Quantum Elements’ digital-twin software and error-management tools to jointly optimize hardware and chemistry workflows. The companies aim to build a validated prototype, benchmark chemistry models and quantum algorithms to investigate how quantum computing could complement existing catalyst simulation methods. PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum today announced they have been selected by the Israel-U.S. Binational Industrial Research and Development (BIRD) Foundation to jointly develop a quantum simulation platform for understanding and designing the chemical reactions that occur on material surfaces. The project, one of seven approved by the BIRD Foundation, has a budget of $2.4 million. The project will combine Qarakal Quantum’s modular superconducting quantum hardware and hardware-software co-design approach with Quantum Elements’ software for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing, using AI-driven co-design, error suppression, error correction and decoders. Together, the companies will work toward a validated prototype capable of taking industrially relevant catalyst problems and turning them into quantum-ready computational workflows. items.headline: Satellite images reveal expanding oil spill off UAE’s Umm Al Quwain coast
items.title: Satellite images show oil spill on UAE coast
items.scifi_hook: Space‑borne eyes track a growing slick threatening Gulf shorelines.
items.eli5: New satellite pictures show oil spreading along the UAE coast after a tanker was hit.
items.why: Visual evidence helps authorities target cleanup and assess environmental damage.
items.text: Newly released satellite images show the widening of the early October oil tanker spill off the shores of the northern emirate of Umm Al Quwain in the United Arab Emirates. While authorities have not confirmed what caused the spill or which tanker it came from, shipping sources say it was struck by an “unidentified projectile.” Experts believe the affected tanker was the Gem No.2. Authorities temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain since Oct. 23 as oil reached closer to the shorelines. Efforts are underway to contain the leak, according to the UAE. The UAE’s Climate Change and Environment Ministry will assess the environmental impacts. Attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf waters have been on the rise since the US- and Israeli-led conflict with Iran.
